input: It is widely understood that boiling is one of those everyday phenomena that appear simple on the surface while resting on a surprisingly subtle foundation, and a closer look at what is happening at the molecular level repays the effort. When a pure component sits at its boiling point, the liquid and the vapour are in a state of phase equilibrium, which means that neither phase is growing at the expense of the other. The condition that defines this state can be put into words as the equality of the chemical potential of the component across the phases: the chemical potential in the liquid is exactly the same as the chemical potential in the vapour. The chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of how strongly the molecules of the component tend to escape from the phase they currently occupy. If the chemical potential in the liquid were higher than in the vapour, molecules would stream out of the liquid and the vapour would grow; if it were lower, the traffic would run the other way and the vapour would condense back into liquid. Only when the two are equal does the net traffic fall to zero, even though molecules continue to cross the interface in both directions at matching rates. At the boiling point, this delicate balance is maintained while vapour bubbles form throughout the body of the liquid, and heat that is supplied at constant pressure goes into converting liquid into vapour rather than into raising the temperature, which consequently stays fixed until one of the phases has disappeared altogether. It is also worth noting that, for a pure component, the boiling point is set by the pressure, since only one temperature at that pressure can make the two chemical potentials come out equal.
target: Phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point is the state in which the liquid and vapour phases coexist and neither phase grows at the expense of the other. The equilibrium condition is stated in words as the equality of the chemical potential of the component across the phases: the chemical potential in the liquid equals the chemical potential in the vapour. The chemical potential measures the tendency of the component to leave the phase it is in. Where the chemical potential in the liquid stands higher than in the vapour, molecules pass from liquid to vapour and the vapour phase grows; where it stands lower, vapour condenses and the liquid phase grows. Transfer continues until the two values meet, and at equality the net transfer stops, although molecules continue to cross the surface in both directions at equal rates. At the boiling point this balance holds while bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid, not only at its surface. Heat supplied at constant pressure then changes the amounts of the two phases rather than the temperature: liquid becomes vapour at a fixed temperature until one phase is gone. The same condition governs condensation, read in the reverse direction, and evaporation from an open surface, where the vapour above the liquid is continually removed and equilibrium is approached but not held. The boiling point itself is fixed by the pressure for a pure component, because only one temperature at that pressure makes the two chemical potentials equal. A pure component has a single boiling point at a given pressure precisely because the equality can be met at only one temperature there. Equilibrium is therefore a condition on the state of the two phases, stated without any measured data, and every boiling, condensation, or flash calculation for a pure component starts from it.
